drives splanchnic arterial vasodilation via local overproduction of nitric oxide, prostacyclin, and endocannabinoids — worsened by bacterial translocation across a leaky gut wall that triggers systemic inflammation.","This pools blood in the splanchnic bed, dropping effective arterial blood volume even though total body volume (and often total body sodium/water) is expanded — the cirrhotic patient is simultaneously volume-overloaded and intravascularly 'underfilled.'","The body senses this as hypovolemia and mounts a maximal neurohormonal response: renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), sympathetic nervous system, and antidiuretic hormone (ADH) all activate to preserve perfusion pressure.","These same systems constrict the renal afferent arteriole, dropping glomerular filtration rate (GFR) despite structurally normal kidneys — this is why HRS is a purely functional/hemodynamic lesion, not acute tubular necrosis (ATN), and is classically reversible with liver transplant.","Precipitants that push this fragile balance over the edge: spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP), GI bleed, over-diuresis, large-volume paracentesis without albumin replacement, and an innocent bystander constricted by the body's own compensatory RAAS/sympathetic/ADH surge, which is exactly why volume expansion (albumin) plus splanchnic vasoconstriction (terlipressin) reverses it.","teaching_pearl":"Think of HRS as 'the kidney is fine, the plumbing upstream is the problem' — the entire treatment strategy is built on redistributing blood volume back into the effective circulation, not fixing an intrinsically damaged nephron.","board_tip":"NSAIDs are absolutely contraindicated in decompensated cirrhosis — they remove the last compensatory afferent arteriolar vasodilation keeping the kidney perfused [1]."},{"heading":"Clinical Findings & Workup: Confirming HRS-AKI vs Its Mimics","minutes":"2-3 min","points":["Diagnosis is one of exclusion using International Club of Ascites (ICA) criteria: rise in creatinine (Cr) ≥0.3 mg/dL within 48h OR ≥50% from baseline, in a patient with cirrhosis and ascites, WITHOUT response to 48h of diuretic withdrawal plus albumin challenge (1 g/kg/day, max 100 g/day) [4].","Must exclude shock, ongoing nephrotoxin exposure, and structural kidney disease — check urinalysis (should be bland, no significant proteinuria/hematuria) and renal ultrasound (should be normal, no obstruction/parenchymal disease).","Serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) ≥1.1 g/dL confirms the ascites is portal-hypertensive in origin, supporting the overall physiologic framework even though it doesn't directly diagnose HRS [1].","Always rule out and treat SBP first — send diagnostic paracentesis; ascitic fluid polymorphonuclear (PMN) count ≥250/mm³ is diagnostic and SBP is the single most common precipitant of HRS [1].","Distinguishing HRS from ATN clinically: ATN typically follows a clear nephrotoxic/ischemic insult and shows muddy brown casts or significant proteinuria on urinalysis; HRS has a bland sediment and occurs in the specific hemodynamic setting above — biomarkers like urinary NGAL are being studied but are not yet standard of care."],"mechanism":"The albumin challenge is diagnostic AND mechanistic: if renal function improves, the problem was reversible effective hypovolemia (prerenal/HRS spectrum); if it doesn't, you're looking at ATN or another structural process — this bedside physiology test is what actually separates the two.","teaching_pearl":"Never diagnose HRS without a paracentesis first — treating presumed HRS while missing untreated SBP is a common and costly error, since SBP itself is the top precipitant.","board_tip":"HRS-AKI is a diagnosis of exclusion built entirely on physiology, not a single lab value — boards will test whether you rule out obstruction, ATN, and SBP before committing to the diagnosis [4]."},{"heading":"Treatment: Reversing the Hemodynamics Per AASLD 2021 Practice Guidance","minutes":"3 min","points":["First-line per AASLD 2021 Practice Guidance: terlipressin plus albumin [1]. Terlipressin is a vasopressin V1 receptor agonist causing selective splanchnic arterial vasoconstriction — it directly reverses the mechanism above by redistributing blood volume out of the splanchnic bed into the effective circulation, suppressing RAAS/sympathetic drive, and restoring renal perfusion pressure.","Albumin is co-administered both as an oncotic volume expander and for its non-oncotic effects (binding circulating NO precursors/cytokines, stabilizing endothelium) — it is never given as monotherapy for HRS.","Terlipressin was FDA-approved in 2022 (brand Terlivaz) based on the CONFIRM trial, which showed significantly higher HRS reversal with terlipressin + albumin vs placebo + albumin (~32% vs ~17%), though with a boxed warning for respiratory failure/hypoxia — avoid in patients with ACLF grade 3, severe hypoxemia, or recent cardiopulmonary compromise [2,3].","Where terlipressin is unavailable, the alternative regimen is midodrine (alpha-1 agonist, systemic vasoconstriction) plus octreotide (suppresses splanchnic vasodilatory hormones like glucagon) plus albumin — mechanistically similar goal (splanchnic vasoconstriction) but historically less potent than terlipressin [1].","Stop diuretics immediately upon diagnosis — they worsen the underlying effective hypovolemia driving the syndrome [1].","Liver transplantation is the only definitive treatment because it eliminates the portal hypertension and splanchnic vasodilation driving the entire cascade; renal function typically recovers post-transplant unless HRS has been prolonged enough to cause secondary ATN, in which case simultaneous liver-kidney transplant is considered per OPTN policy for patients requiring dialysis for an extended duration.","Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) directly lowers portal pressure and can help select patients but is generally avoided in high MELD/high bilirubin patients due to hepatic encephalopathy and liver failure risk [1]."],"mechanism":"Terlipressin works by directly reversing the splanchnic vasodilation that started the whole cascade — constrict the splanchnic bed, restore effective arterial volume, turn off RAAS/sympathetic/ADH, and the renal afferent arteriole relaxes, restoring GFR. Albumin ensures the redistributed volume has adequate oncotic support to stay in the vascular space.","teaching_pearl":"Terlipressin plus albumin doesn't fix the kidney — it fixes the plumbing upstream that was strangling the kidney; that's why response is judged by hemodynamic reversal (creatinine trend), not by any direct renal intervention.","board_tip":"Know the boxed warning: terlipressin carries a real risk of serious or fatal respiratory failure, so screen for hypoxia and ACLF grade 3 before starting per the CONFIRM trial safety signal [2,3]."},{"heading":"Outcomes & Prognosis","minutes":"1-2 min","points":["Untreated HRS-AKI (formerly HRS type 1) carries a median survival of only weeks without treatment — historically one of the most lethal complications of decompensated cirrhosis [1].","With terlipressin + albumin, HRS reversal occurs in roughly 30-40% of patients (CONFIRM: ~32% vs 17% placebo), improving short-term renal outcomes though overall mortality benefit has been less consistently demonstrated across trials [2].","Liver transplantation remains the only therapy that changes the natural history — post-transplant 1-year survival for patients transplanted with HRS is generally comparable to non-HRS cirrhotic transplant recipients when renal function recovers, underscoring transplant as the true definitive treatment [1].","Prognosis is worse with higher MELD score, concurrent SBP or ACLF, and delay in recognizing/treating the precipitant — early paracentesis and prompt albumin/antibiotic therapy for SBP meaningfully reduce HRS incidence [1]."}],"summary_points":["HRS is a functional renal failure driven by splanchnic arterial vasodilation from portal HTN, causing effective hypovolemia and compensatory RAAS/sympathetic/ADH-mediated renal vasoconstriction — the kidney itself is structurally normal.","Diagnosis is by exclusion (ICA criteria): rising Cr despite diuretic withdrawal and an albumin challenge, bland urinalysis, normal renal ultrasound, and always after ruling out SBP via paracentesis.","First-line treatment per AASLD 2021 Practice Guidance is terlipressin plus albumin, which mechanistically reverses splanchnic vasodilation and restores effective arterial volume; {"title":"Diabetic Ketoacidosis: Knowing When the Crisis Is Actually Over","subtitle":"Managing the insulin infusion when glucose falls before the anion gap closes","guideline_sources":["ADA/EASD Consensus Report on Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes (2024)","ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes (2025)"],"references":[{"id":1,"source":"Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report (ADA/EASD)","year":2024,"society":"ADA/EASD","url":"https://doi.org/10.2337/dci24-0032","type":"consensus statement"},{"id":2,"source":"Standards of Care in Diabetes—2025, Section 16: Diabetes Care in the Hospital","year":2025,"society":"American Diabetes Association","url":"https://diabetesjournals.org/care/issue/48/Supplement_1","type":"guideline"}],"question":{"stem":"A 24-year-old woman is evaluated in the ICU for diabetic ketoacidosis. She has type 1 diabetes managed with an insulin pump and presented 6 hours ago with 2 days of vomiting after her infusion set became dislodged. She was given 0.9% saline and a weight-based intravenous regular insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/h; her current fluids contain 20 mEq/L potassium chloride. Her vomiting has stopped, but she has not yet eaten.

Temperature 36.9 C, BP 116/70 mm Hg, HR 92/min, RR 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air. She is alert and oriented. Mucous membranes are moist, and capillary refill is normal.

Repeat studies: glucose 184 mg/dL, sodium 137 mEq/L, potassium 4.1 mEq/L, chloride 105 mEq/L, bicarbonate 13 mEq/L, BUN 16 mg/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, venous pH 7.25, beta-hydroxybutyrate 4.1 mmol/L.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?","choices":[{"letter":"A","text":"Add 5% dextrose to intravenous fluids","correct":true},{"letter":"B","text":"Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate","correct":false},{"letter":"C","text":"Decrease insulin infusion rate by 50%","correct":false},{"letter":"D","text":"Discontinue insulin infusion and start subcutaneous glargine","correct":false},{"letter":"E","text":"Increase insulin infusion rate by 50%","correct":false}],"correct_letter":"A","explanation":"Per the 2024 ADA/EASD consensus report on hyperglycemic crises, once plasma glucose falls below approximately 250 mg/dL during DKA treatment, dextrose (5-10%) should be added to the intravenous fluids so that the insulin infusion can be continued at a rate sufficient to suppress ketogenesis without producing hypoglycemia. Insulin — not glucose lowering per se — is what terminates lipolysis and ketone production, and resolution criteria are biochemical: anion gap 12 mEq/L or less, bicarbonate 15-18 mEq/L or greater, pH greater than 7.3, or beta-hydroxybutyrate less than 0.6 mmol/L.

This patient has met none of them: anion gap is 19 mEq/L, bicarbonate 13 mEq/L, pH 7.25, and beta-hydroxybutyrate 4.1 mmol/L. Her glucose has normalized far faster than her ketoacidosis has cleared — the expected pattern, since glucose falls with rehydration and glycosuria while ketone clearance lags. Withholding or truncating insulin now would allow ketogenesis to resume.

Adding dextrose while maintaining the insulin infusion (targeting glucose roughly 150-200 mg/dL until the gap closes) satisfies both requirements. Transition to subcutaneous insulin is appropriate only after ketoacidosis has resolved and the patient is eating, and the basal dose must be given 1-2 hours before the drip is stopped to avoid rebound ketosis [1,2]."},"wrong_explanations":[{"letter":"B","why":"The 2024 ADA/EASD consensus reserves bicarbonate for pH below 7.0, and even then the benefit is uncertain. At pH 7.25 with preserved perfusion, bicarbonate offers no mortality or recovery benefit and risks hypokalemia and paradoxical CNS acidosis."},{"letter":"C","why":"Halving insulin reduces the very hormonal signal needed to shut off ketogenesis. The correct maneuver when glucose falls is to supply dextrose, not to under-dose insulin; premature reduction prolongs the acidosis and risks recurrent DKA."},{"letter":"D","why":"Transition requires resolved ketoacidosis (gap 12 or less, bicarbonate 15-18 or greater, pH above 7.3) plus oral intake. She meets none, has not eaten, and stopping the drip without 1-2 hours of subcutaneous overlap predictably causes rebound ketosis."},{"letter":"E","why":"Escalating insulin without dextrose at a glucose of 184 mg/dL will cause hypoglycemia. Persistent acidosis here reflects the normal lag in ketone clearance, not insulin resistance or an inadequate infusion rate."}],"difficulty_level":4,"difficulty_label":"Board-level","difficulty_rationale":"The solver must recognize that normalized glucose and unresolved ketoacidosis coexist, apply the biochemical resolution criteria rather than the glucose value, and then choose the maneuver that preserves insulin delivery while preventing hypoglycemia — with two closely competing insulin-adjustment distractors.","reasoning_steps":["Calculate the anion gap (137 - 105 - 13 = 19 mEq/L) and note bicarbonate 13, pH 7.25, beta-hydroxybutyrate 4.1 — ketoacidosis is unresolved.","Recognize that glucose 184 mg/dL reflects rehydration and glycosuria, not resolution; glucose normalizes before ketone clearance.","Apply the principle that continued insulin, not glucose control, is what suppresses ketogenesis, so the infusion must not be reduced or stopped.","Apply the 2024 ADA/EASD rule to add 5-10% dextrose once glucose falls below ~250 mg/dL to permit continued insulin without hypoglycemia.","Defer subcutaneous transition until gap closure plus oral intake, with 1-2 hours of drip overlap."]},"key_point":"In DKA, resolution is defined by closure of the anion gap and normalization of bicarbonate/pH — not by glucose; when glucose falls below ~250 mg/dL, add dextrose and continue the insulin infusion [1].","abim_classification":{"category":"Endocrinology","subcategory":"Diabetes Mellitus","specific_topic":"Diabetic ketoacidosis: insulin infusion management and resolution criteria","blueprint_weight":"9%"},"board_pearls":["Insulin suppresses lipolysis and hepatic ketogenesis; glucose lowering is a separate, faster-resolving effect, which is why the infusion must continue after euglycemia is reached — enabled by adding dextrose.","The 2024 ADA/EASD hyperglycemic crises consensus report specifies adding 5-10% dextrose once glucose is below approximately 250 mg/dL and defines DKA resolution as anion gap 12 mEq/L or less, bicarbonate 15-18 mEq/L or greater, pH above 7.3, or beta-hydroxybutyrate below 0.6 mmol/L [1].","The discriminator between continuing insulin with dextrose and transitioning to subcutaneous insulin is the anion gap/beta-hydroxybutyrate, plus whether the patient is eating — never the glucose value alone.","Direct beta-hydroxybutyrate measurement is now preferred over urine ketones or nitroprusside testing for monitoring, since urine acetoacetate can paradoxically rise as beta-hydroxybutyrate is converted during recovery [1].","The classic trap is stopping the infusion when glucose normalizes: without 1-2 hours of overlap with subcutaneous basal insulin and with an open gap, ketogenesis restarts and DKA recurs within hours [1,2]."],"teaching_points":["Two independent monitoring targets exist in DKA: glucose (kept ~150-200 mg/dL with dextrose-containing fluids) and ketoacidosis (followed by anion gap, bicarbonate, pH, or beta-hydroxybutyrate).","Potassium 3.3-5.2 mEq/L warrants 20-30 mEq/L in each liter of fluid; insulin should be held if potassium is below 3.3 mEq/L until replacement is under way, because insulin drives potassium intracellularly.","Euglycemic DKA from SGLT2 inhibitors follows the same rule with even greater force — glucose may never exceed 200 mg/dL, so dextrose plus insulin infusion is required from the outset until the gap closes."],"summary_points":["Continue the insulin infusion and add dextrose when glucose falls below ~250 mg/dL; stop only after biochemical resolution, with subcutaneous overlap [1]."],"visual_memory_card":{"top_left":"Glucose 184 but gap 19, pH 7.25","top_right":"Insulin stops ketogenesis; dextrose prevents hypoglycemia","bottom_left":"Treat the gap, not the glucose","bottom_right":"Stopping drip at euglycemia causes rebound ketosis","center":""}}
